messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time

Vignette:
The fire at the Riverside Arts Center was Elena Vasquez’s first month as its resident painter. Of Mexican and Irish descent, she had always worked with the patient precision her grandmother had taught her, but that afternoon, the back wall gave way and the smoke rolled heavy across the floorboards. She and her husband, David, scrambled toward the service corridor, their hands pressing against hot brick as they waited for rescue. When the firefighters finally pulled them free, she felt her shoulders lock into the exact angle they had held for hours. In the weeks that followed, what happened to her was not a fading narrative but a series of still, high-contrast images flashing in her mind, each one indistinguishable from a photograph. Every time the memories surfaced, a heavy, suffocating guilt settled over her, as if her survival were a theft. Her understanding of how the world operates had been completely shattered. She had come to believe her life was no longer worth living, a quiet conviction that sat beside the realization that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again. The disorder did not announce itself; it accumulated in quiet adjustments. She learned to keep her mind occupied at all times, stretching canvases, organizing her supplies, and working until her hands grew stiff. She tried hard not to think about the center, not about the smoke, not about the silence in the house where David no longer answered. When the quiet grew too loud, she listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home, her hand resting on the back door latch until her knuckles whitened. She could not fall asleep, nor could she stay asleep. Her body kept her awake, rigid and alert. On the days when the weight became too heavy, she allowed herself to cry, the tears coming in sudden, overwhelming waves that left her drained. Irritability took root alongside the exhaustion. She found herself snapping at acquaintances, her voice rising in angry outbursts that surprised her as much as they startled them. She avoided news reports about building fires or industrial accidents, turning screens off before the stories began. When neighbors or gallery owners reached out, she flinched at the physical touch, her breath catching as her muscles braced for impact. Now, at seventy-three, Elena works from a sunlit garage studio where she spent her days grinding pigments and preparing canvases. In that very space, she had long avoided alcohol-based solvents, relying instead on dry brushes and natural binders. One afternoon, as she sorted through a bin of cleaning cloths, the faint trace of rubbing alcohol caught her attention. The smell struck her immediately, and she stepped back, her breath shortening, her body settling back into the cramped posture from the corridor. The guilt rose to meet her, unyielding and immediate. She tells her therapist that she cannot name what she is afraid of anymore, only that she hopes someone can help her find a way to sit in a room without bracing for impact, to sleep without counting breaths, and to look at her own work without feeling that the world no longer makes sense. She came to seek help because the quiet of her house had grown louder than the silence she had carried for years, and she wanted to understand why the memories would not stay still, and why she needed to find a way to live inside her own life again.
